title: Figures, Layout, and Basic Plotting
summary: Learn matplotlib's Figure/Axes object model, how to set figure size and call tight_layout, and how to use plt.plot() in both its one-argument and two-argument forms.

steps.title: The Figure and the Axes
steps.lede: Every matplotlib graph lives inside two nested objects — learn which is which before writing code.

blocks.text: Imagine this week's QuickDeliver delivery times — 18, 22, 26, 19, 30 minutes — as a graph instead of a list. Matplotlib draws that graph onto two different kinds of object. Matplotlib graphs data on Figures, and each Figure can contain one or more Axes, which is the area where data is actually plotted.

The Figure is the overall canvas — the whole window or image you display or save. An Axes is one plotting area inside that Figure: the rectangle with its own x- and y-axis where lines, bars, or points are drawn. A single Figure can hold more than one Axes.
After `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt`, `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` creates a Figure and one Axes together: `fig` refers to the whole canvas, `ax` refers to the plotting area inside it.

blocks.title: Figure contains Axes
blocks.alt_text: A box-within-a-box diagram: the outer rectangle is labelled 'Figure (canvas)'; inside it sits a smaller rectangle labelled 'Axes (plotting area)'; inside the Axes a simple line represents plotted data.

segments.summary: The presenter defines the three-level hierarchy: a Figure is the top-level container — the entire window or page — while an Axes (spelled with an 'e') is the actual plot area where a specific piece of data is drawn, and a single Figure can hold multiple Axes. segments.label: Creating a Figure and one Axes explicitly with plt.subplots()
segments.summary: The presenter recaps that the Figure is the container holding all plots — the whole window — and that Axes are the actual plots inside it, with a Figure able to hold more than one. They then introduce the object-oriented approach: writing fig, ax = plt.subplots() instantiates both a Figure and an Axes at once. Because no row or column count is passed, subplots defaults to a one-by-one grid, producing exactly one Axes assigned to ax.

steps.title: Plotting onto the Axes
steps.lede: All drawing goes through ax — not fig.

blocks.text: Plotting calls such as `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto that Axes object. After `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`, `ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` draws the delivery times as a line onto `ax`. The Figure never receives plotted data — it just holds the Axes.

steps.title: Figure or Axes?
steps.lede: Choose the right object for each plotting task.

public.prompt: After running `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`, you want to draw a line of QuickDeliver delivery times. Which object do you call `.plot()` on?

options.text: Either `fig` or `ax` — they both hold the same data

opt_ax.message: Correct. Plotting calls such as `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto the Axes object — the rectangle with its own x- and y-axis where data is actually rendered.

opt_fig.message: Not quite. The Figure is the overall canvas — it holds the Axes but never receives plotted data directly. Plotting calls go on `ax`, not `fig`.

opt_plt.message: Not quite. `plt.plot()` is a different function from `ax.plot()`. When you have an explicit `ax` variable from `plt.subplots()`, you call `ax.plot()` to draw onto that specific Axes.

opt_either.message: Not quite. Only the Axes (`ax`) receives plotted data. The Figure (`fig`) is the canvas that contains the Axes — it does not hold data itself.

correct.message: Exactly right. The Axes is the plotting area — all drawing calls go on `ax`.

incorrect.message: Remember: `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` gives you two objects. The Figure (`fig`) is the canvas; the Axes (`ax`) is where data is drawn. Plotting calls go on `ax`.

hints: Think about which object is described as 'the rectangle with its own x- and y-axis where data is drawn'.
`plt.subplots()` returns two values — the first is the canvas, the second is the plotting area.

steps.title: Create a Figure and Plot on Its Axes

The figure should contain exactly one Axes with one line whose x-values are `days` and y-values are `delivery_times`.

steps.title: Setting Figure Size and Fitting the Layout
steps.lede: Two settings on the Figure object control how big it is and whether its contents fit without clipping.

blocks.text: `plt.subplots(figsize=(width, height))` sets the figure's dimensions. `figsize` is a (width, height) tuple measured in inches; its default is [6.4, 4.8]. Passing `figsize=(8, 4)` makes a wider-than-default figure, 8 inches by 4 inches.

`tight_layout()` automatically adjusts subplot parameters so the subplot(s) fit into the figure area; it checks the extents of tick labels, axis labels, and titles. Call it as `plt.tight_layout()` or `fig.tight_layout()`.

blocks.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
fig.tight_layout()

annotations.text: figsize=(8, 4) sets the canvas to 8 inches wide by 4 inches tall
fig.tight_layout() adjusts spacing so subplot contents fit within the figure area

steps.title: Fitting the Layout
steps.lede: Which call adjusts subplot spacing so labels don't get clipped?

public.prompt: You have created a figure with `fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))`. Which of the following is true about calling `tight_layout`?

options.text: `fig.tight_layout()` is the only correct way to call `tight_layout`
`plt.tight_layout()` is the only correct way to call `tight_layout`

opt_fig_tight.message: Not quite. `fig.tight_layout()` is a valid call, but it is not the only way. `plt.tight_layout()` also adjusts subplot spacing — both forms are correct.

opt_plt_tight.message: Not quite. `plt.tight_layout()` is a valid call, but it is not the only way. `fig.tight_layout()` also adjusts subplot spacing — both forms are correct.

opt_both.message: Correct. `tight_layout()` can be called as `plt.tight_layout()` or `fig.tight_layout()` — both automatically adjust subplot parameters so the subplot fits into the figure area.

opt_ax_tight.message: Incorrect. `tight_layout()` is a Figure-level method, not an Axes method. Call it as `fig.tight_layout()` or `plt.tight_layout()`, not on `ax`.

correct.message: Right! `tight_layout()` can be called on the figure object (`fig.tight_layout()`) or via pyplot (`plt.tight_layout()`) — both work.

incorrect.message: `tight_layout()` is a Figure-level operation. It can be called as `fig.tight_layout()` or `plt.tight_layout()` — both adjust subplot spacing automatically.

hints: The fact says `tight_layout()` can be called in two ways — one uses the `fig` variable, the other uses `plt` directly.
`tight_layout()` is not a method on the Axes (`ax`) — it operates on the Figure.

steps.title: Two Ways to Call plt.plot()
steps.lede: pyplot's `plot()` function accepts data in two forms — learn which x-axis you get from each.

blocks.text: You have already seen `ax.plot(x, y)` draw onto an Axes created with `plt.subplots()`. pyplot also has its own `plot()` function, called directly as `plt.plot()`, and it accepts data in two different forms.

`plt.plot(y)` with a single argument treats it as y-values and automatically generates x-values starting from 0. `plt.plot([18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots those five delivery times against the automatic x-positions 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

`plt.plot(x, y)` with two arguments plots y-values against the given x-values instead. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` plots the same delivery times against day numbers 1 through 5, not the automatic 0-based positions.

annotations.text: Single argument: y-values only; x starts at 0
Two arguments: x-values first, then y-values

blocks.takeaway: Both forms call the same function; the only difference is whether you supply x-values or let pyplot number them from 0.

steps.title: Two ways to call plt.plot(): supplying x and y vs. y alone

The instructor then demonstrates the single-argument form: passing only the y-values list, with the note that plt.plot() defaults to starting at zero and stepping by one for the x-positions, so the x-axis is filled in automatically.

steps.title: One Argument or Two?
steps.lede: Identify which plt.plot() form produces which x-axis.

public.prompt: You call `plt.plot([18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` with a single list argument. What x-values does matplotlib use for the plot?

options.text: No x-axis is drawn — a single argument produces a bar chart instead

opt_auto_0.message: Correct. `plt.plot(y)` with a single argument treats the list as y-values and automatically generates x-positions starting from 0 (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 for five values).

opt_auto_1.message: Not quite. The automatic x-positions start from 0, not 1. For five y-values, matplotlib uses x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

opt_values.message: Not quite. The single argument is treated as y-values, not x-values. Matplotlib generates its own x-positions starting from 0.

opt_none.message: Not quite. `plt.plot()` draws a line by default. With a single argument it uses the list as y-values and auto-generates x-positions from 0.

correct.message: Exactly right. `plt.plot(y)` auto-generates x-positions starting at 0 — so five values get x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

incorrect.message: `plt.plot(y)` treats its single argument as y-values and fills in x-positions automatically starting from 0. To supply your own x-values, use `plt.plot(x, y)` with two arguments.

steps.title: What You've Learned
steps.lede: Three concepts, one workflow: create a Figure, size it, and plot onto its Axes.

blocks.text: With `plt.subplots()` you get a Figure and an Axes first, then call a plotting method on the Axes, not the Figure. Figure is the canvas; Axes is where data goes. Set `figsize` to control canvas dimensions and call `tight_layout()` to prevent labels from clipping.
Both `plt.plot(y)` and `plt.plot(x, y)` call the same function; the only difference is whether you supply x-values or let pyplot number them from 0.

remediation_steps.title: Figure vs. Axes — Which Object Does What?
remediation_steps.lede: A quick contrast to clarify which object is the canvas and which one receives your data.

blocks.text: The Figure is the outer canvas — the whole window. The Axes is the inner plotting area where data is drawn. `fig, ax = plt.subplots()` creates both at once: `fig` is the canvas, `ax` is the plotting area. Plotting calls like `ax.plot(x, y)` go on `ax`, never on `fig`.

remediation_steps.title: tight_layout() — What It Does and How to Call It
remediation_steps.lede: A clear contrast between calling tight_layout and not calling it.

blocks.text: `tight_layout()` automatically adjusts subplot parameters so the subplot(s) fit into the figure area; it checks the extents of tick labels, axis labels, and titles. Without it, labels can be clipped or overlap. Call it as `plt.tight_layout()` or `fig.tight_layout()` — both work.

remediation_steps.title: plt.plot() — One Argument vs. Two
remediation_steps.lede: The x-axis is the only thing that changes between the two forms.

blocks.text: `plt.plot([18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` uses one argument: the list is treated as y-values and x-positions are filled in automatically starting at 0 (so 0, 1, 2, 3, 4). `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [18, 22, 26, 19, 30])` uses two arguments: the first list sets the x-axis to 1–5, the second sets the y-axis. Both calls produce a line; only the x-axis differs.
